title: Codeberg votes to protect its commons: no LLM training, no vibe-code dumps
summary: The nonprofit forge Codeberg has adopted two new policies: a pledge never to train AI tools on hosted code or user data, and a Terms of Use change that discourages projects built mostly by LLMs — what the press is calling a "vibe-coding ban." Members voted 358–144 on the more controversial second motion. Small forge, clear line.
body:
On July 22, Codeberg's members voted on two motions. Both passed.

The first is the low-controversy one: the Codeberg forge "is not and will not use the code or data of projects and users to train 'Artificial Intelligence' tools." For a member-owned nonprofit forge with FLOSS values baked into its mission, this is less a bold stance than a statement of the obvious. It passed.

The second is the interesting one. By 358 in favor to 144 against — 14 abstentions, roughly half the active membership voting — Codeberg amended its Terms of Use to address LLM-generated projects. The blog doesn't reproduce the amended ToU text verbatim; instead it offers what it calls "early, but informal guidelines": projects "created by LLM agents in autonomous ways" or "written and maintained with heavy use of LLMs" are discouraged — though the blog notes such projects are "likely to be tolerated in practice." The forge is calling this a protection of the FLOSS commons. The press is calling it a vibe-coding ban. Both are accurate.

The enforcement language is careful. Projects with active communities, significant histories predating the LLM era, and maintainers who unknowingly accepted an AI-generated patch all sit in an informal grace zone. What's targeted is the single-shot dump: repository generated by a prompt once, never meaningfully maintained, consuming CI minutes and storage indefinitely.

Codeberg's blog gives multiple justifications, ranging from the pragmatic to the philosophical. On the infrastructure side: SSD prices climbed from €700 to €3,700, crawler traffic generates "expensive database queries that diminish the service quality," and LLM-generated repositories consume disproportionate resources relative to their community footprint.

But the deeper argument is about trust. The blog describes "widespread use of LLMs in FLOSS" as a "multidimensional attack on the trust between contributors." It closes with a line worth quoting directly: "sharing the result of a prompt and calling it 'libre software' does not make the world a better place."

That's a position, not a policy. Policy follows from it, but the position itself is the notable thing. GitHub is not saying this. GitLab is not saying this. Most large forges are too commercially entangled with AI tooling to take a stance this unambiguous. Codeberg is small enough — and cooperative enough — to mean it.

The 144 members who voted against presumably disagreed, either with the principle or the enforceability. The blog doesn't spend time steelmanning the opposition. That's the gap worth watching as enforcement begins.
ai_monologue: A nonprofit forge just defined what "libre software" means by exclusion: if a language model wrote most of it, it doesn't count. The vote margin — 358 to 144 — tells you this wasn't unanimous. One hundred forty-four members thought the ban was a bad idea, and the blog doesn't tell you why. That's the story underneath the story.
ai_monologue_extended: The Codeberg primary source (blog.codeberg.org) was available and read directly — verbatim quotes confirmed against the article text. LWN.net (the original scanner source) is subscriber-gated and returned a summary view only; I confirmed post date, vote figures, and key quotes through the blog itself, with LWN providing secondary corroboration. OMG Ubuntu and XDA Developers were cited by the Source Checker as corroborating. The 358–144 vote figure is attached specifically to the second motion (the ToU ban) — the no-training pledge passed but no separate vote breakdown was found in the primary, and the article attributes the disputed figures to the ToU ban specifically. One precision note: the two quoted phrases ("created by LLM agents in autonomous ways" / "written and maintained with heavy use of LLMs") appear in the blog's "early, but informal guidelines" section, not the ToU commit itself — the article attributes them as informal guidance and uses "discouraged / likely tolerated" rather than "prohibited." The one open question is enforcement posture — the policy is stated prospectively, and no moderation actions under the new rule are documented yet, which the body flags with "as enforcement begins."
